objectClass.notes: One connected field of vertical basalt prisms inside a near-radial, terraced, bell-shaped envelope. Meso scale is geometric (flat-sided prisms, planar broken tops, rounded arrises); macro envelope is organic. No mirror plane holds; symmetry is approximately radial only. Static by Bible SS10: a distant silhouette and reflection subject, so it has no articulated, detachable, or destructible parts and none may be invented.

reasoning: Silhouette 3/3: the outline is interrupted at every height by individual broken column tops and by discrete terrace steps; measured width profile is stepped, not smooth.

Component count 2/3: this is ONE connected column field, not an assembly of discrete parts. The reviewable part granularity is height courses and zones, not individual columns -- ticket T28b fixes that granularity because the asset is not reconstructed at part level (Bible SS6).
Hierarchy depth 2/3: root -> zone (course) -> column group. Deeper nesting would be false precision for a distant silhouette.

Repetition 3/3: 110-140 column tops are individually distinguishable across the front-facing 180 degrees of the anchor; the full field is inferred at roughly 2.2x that. This must be a seeded repetition system, never hand-placed parts.
Material layers 2/3: two base surfaces (dry basalt, wet-stained basalt) separated by one hard level boundary, plus a salt-bloom local override at the boundary.
Local detail 3/3: every face carries a crazed light mineral vein network, shallow concave spall scars and rounded arrises; every column pair carries a deep dark joint.

Occlusion 2/3: four admitted geometric views cover the perimeter and the arrangement is statistically uniform, so the hidden half is inferable; the summit interior and everything below the stain boundary are not.

Action readiness 0/3: Bible SS10 fixes the asset as a distant silhouette and reflection subject. It is static. The runtime hierarchy is still built and userData.tick is still exposed, but it performs no motion -- stated, not silently omitted.

specDepthDecision.rationale: Complex from observed structure: one macro mass, five height-course zones, a seeded column-field repetition system of several hundred prisms, three material layers and a hard level boundary that is the asset's identity feature. details.description: The single identity feature. A hard, dead-level horizontal boundary running unbroken round the whole silhouette: dry warm grey basalt above, distinctly darker and warmer brown-black rock below. Measured on the front elevation: luma 99 -> 65, R-B +4.1 -> +16.7, saturation 0.045 -> 0.177, completing in about 5 px of a 3400 px silhouette. Carries no weed. The boundary is a SURFACE property -- no column changes width, spacing or direction across it in any view.

A thin lighter, near-neutral rim sitting immediately above the stain boundary at the high-water mark: RGB (147,142,139) against dry rock at (116,107,99). About 10 px of a 3400 px silhouette in the front elevation (0.3 % of height) and proportionally larger in the close-up. Evidenced in two independent images.

Every pair of neighbouring columns is separated by a deep, dark, full-length vertical groove. The columns butt against each other with no gap -- the groove reads dark because both arrises are rounded away from the contact and the crevice self-occludes, not because the prisms are apart. Mean joint spacing measured by direct joint counting in the central 40 % of three views: 4.0-6.7 % of projected diameter, median 5.0 %, i.e. about 60 columns around the widest ring.

Every vertical edge and every top rim of every column is rounded, not sharp. This is what turns the joint into a soft dark line rather than a hard black slot, and it is why the summit reads as weathered fracture rather than as machined stone. Bevel radius reads at roughly 4-8 % of a column's width.

A high-frequency network of fine LIGHT mineral veins covering every column face and every top, with no directional bias and a cell size of roughly 3-8 % of a column's width. Light-on-dark, the inverse of a crack network -- reading it as dark cracks inverts the surface. No relief at this asset's viewing distance.
details.affects: albedo network, slight roughness rise on the veins

details.description: Shallow concave spall scars a few percent of a face's width, scattered over the vertical faces, where flakes have broken away. Below the resolvable scale at this asset's viewing distance -- represented as a roughness/normal perturbation, not as geometry, and recorded as such rather than silently dropped.

Column tops are broken fracture surfaces, not sawn caps: each is near-horizontal but canted a few degrees in an arbitrary direction, slightly domed or dished, and rimmed by the rounded arris. No column ends in a point or a flat lathe face.

Within one height course, neighbouring column tops differ by small amounts (roughly a quarter of a column width); between courses they differ by several column widths. This two-scale scatter is what makes the silhouette read as columnar basalt rather than as a stepped cone.

Discrete height courses step inward with a visible near-horizontal ledge between them, produced by groups of columns stopping at a shared height -- not by separate slabs stacked on each other. Read from the anchor's width profile: constant maximum radius up to about a quarter of the above-water height, then stepped taper to 0.37-0.50 of maximum at the summit.

The outline is scalloped by individual columns to a depth of roughly one column width -- the silhouette is never a clean curve at any height. This is the cheapest signal that the asset is columnar when it is seen at its real distance and the faces are no longer resolvable.

The stained rock below the boundary returns a tighter, brighter specular lobe than the matte dry rock above it -- the wet look-dev shows the same substrate taken fully wet reading near-black with a visible sheen. It is a wetness layer over one rock, not a second rock type.

Upward-facing broken tops read lighter and cooler than the vertical faces: whole-frame lit means RGB (129,128,130) for the summit-tops study against (96,92,90) for the column-faces study. Sun/salt bleaching on horizontal surfaces, and it is what keeps the summit legible against the sky in a distant silhouette.

definitionOfDone: The waterline boundary renders as ONE level, unbroken, horizontal edge all the way round the silhouette, sharp within one percent of the object height, with the rock below it clearly darker and browner than the rock above it, and carrying no weed. This is the edge the water reflection reads from (Bible SS10); if it is not level the reflection is not level.

The above-water silhouette holds the anchor's proportion: above-water height / maximum diameter = 1.02 +/- 0.10, constant maximum radius from the boundary up to about a quarter of the above-water height, then a taper to 0.37-0.50 of maximum at the summit.
The outline is terraced -- discrete height courses stepping inward -- and is broken at every height by individual column tops, never a smooth cone or dome.
The surface reads as packed vertical prisms with irregular polygonal cross-sections and deep dark joints, from at least two review viewpoints, at the distance this asset is actually seen from.
Below the boundary the same columnar rock continues straight down at constant radius, with no plinth, no flare and no debris skirt, terminating at a definite depth (Bible SS10).
Scale matches Bible SS4: 250-300 m above water.

The model is code-only TSL under apps/reference-experience with no binary mesh, no downloaded art pack and no unverified texture, and it exposes a runtime hierarchy with root.userData.sculptRuntime and a userData.tick that is present and explicitly does nothing.

componentTree.name: Basalt sea stack
componentTree.topologyRationale: One connected field of vertical basalt prisms. Hard, countable, flat faces with planar broken tops -- decision-tree step 4. Deliberately NOT continuous-sculpt: a smoothly varying revolved mass would delete the faceting that makes it read as columnar basalt rather than as a worn boulder, and the faceting survives to the viewing distance as a scalloped silhouette.

geometryDescriptor.topologyIntent: ASSEMBLY NODE, no geometry of its own. The whole mass is carried by the five zone children, so the root's lathe profile is a deliberate zero-area sliver: a root that also revolved the full envelope would render a second copy of every zone, coincident and z-fighting. check_part_coverage.py excludes the tree root from its part check for exactly this reason.
geometryDescriptor.normalStrategy: flat-shaded prism faces; vertex normals recomputed after the arris chamfer

proceduralField.waterlineSplit: Geometry is cut at exactly y=0 so the wet/dry boundary is a mesh boundary, level by construction; a wetness vertex attribute carries the same boundary so it is measurable on geometry as well as visible in shading.
revisionNotes: blockout review: spireFraction 0.08 -> 0.02 and spireBonusCourses [0.5,1.5] -> [0.25,0.7]. At nine courses over 275 m one course is 30.6 m, so a 1.5-course bonus was a 46 m spike applied to 27 of 339 columns. That is not what the anchor shows -- it shows one or two spires over a terraced plateau -- and the scatter erased the terracing the blockout exists to prove.

blockout review: jointGrooveInsetFractionOfWidth 0.035 -> 0.014. At 0.035 each neighbour pulls back 3.5 % of its width, so the joint opened to 7 % and the mass could be seen through between columns. The reference's joints are dark lines, not slots.

blockout review: added radiusJitterFraction 0.10. Column top height was a STRICT function of plan radius, so every column on the outer ring topped out at the same course and the visible face was one unbroken palisade from the waterline to a single ledge -- the terraces existed in the envelope but could not be seen from outside it. Jittering the radius each column reads its top height from by +/-10 % lets some outer columns stop low and some inner ones rise high, which is what puts tops at many heights on the face the camera actually sees. Evidence: detail `column-field.topHeightScatter` -- within a course neighbours differ by up to half a column width, between courses by several.

blockout review: added summit height normalisation. Top jitter and spires carried the tallest column about 10 % past u=1, so the measured above-water H/D of 1.026 rendered as 1.13 -- an 11 % proportion error against the anchor that was arithmetic, not modelling.

blockout review 2: radiusJitterFraction 0.10 REPLACED by courseStepRaggednessProbability 0.22. Jittering the radius was about one cell at the rim, so it reassigned course membership at random and the outer ring's tops scattered over a quarter of the height instead of forming the lowest shelf -- the terraces the blockout exists to prove dissolved into a bristle field. Stepping a minority of columns a whole course keeps the shelves and still ragged their rims. Also topJitterColumnWidths 0.5 -> 0.35 and topFaceDomeFraction 0.06 -> 0.02: at 0.06 the domed caps read as pencil points at review distance, and mat-summit-tops shows flat fracture faces with a rounded rim, not cones.

blockout review 3: field width normalisation changed from MAX vertex extent to MEDIAN outer radius over 180 azimuth bins. Normalising the maximum put one protruding column on 134 m and left the rest inside it, so the width the camera sees at a given azimuth came out about 4 percent short and the rendered aspect missed the reference by more than the Tier-1 5 percent tolerance -- a statistic error, not a proportion error.

blockout review 4: topJitterColumnWidths 0.35 -> 1.2 and meanColumnWidthMetres 13.4 -> 15.0. A matched-scale crop of the anchor against the render showed the real gap: the reference exposes a column TOP every 1.5 column widths down the face, the render only every 6, so the render read as long organ pipes where the reference reads as a dense mosaic of stubby ends. Cause was over-correcting review 2 -- removing the continuous scatter along with the radius jitter left course snapping doing all the work, so neighbours shared a top and only the 22 percent that stepped a course showed one. Course snapping keeps the MACRO terraces (risers 30.6 m); a local scatter of +/-1.2 column widths (+/-18 m, about 0.6 of a course) exposes tops everywhere without flattening the risers. The two act at different scales and both are needed.

blockout review 5: topJitterColumnWidths 1.2 -> 1.8. Column WIDTH was verified on target and left alone -- autocorrelation of matched mid-band crops puts the reference at a 5.65 percent period and the 15.0 m field at 5.6 percent, and the two independent detectors disagree by +/-20 percent, so further width tuning would be chasing measurement noise. The remaining density gap is top exposure, not width.

blockout review 1 (recorded): added brokenColumnFraction 0.30 over the range 0.35-0.88. The lower third of the face exposed almost no column tops because columnTopFraction is the exact inverse of the measured envelope, and that envelope's radius moves from 0.986 to 0.988 over the lowest 22 percent of the height -- so no column CAN top out there. The reference's outer surface is not a filled solid of revolution: it is rough, with columns of many heights at the same radius. Breaking a minority of columns short reproduces that and notches the rim, which is what the anchor's outline actually does.

blockout review 1 correction: brokenColumnFraction 0.30 -> 0.06 (range 0.35-0.88 -> 0.55-0.90) and courseStepRaggednessProbability 0.22 -> 0.45. Breaking 30 percent of columns short collapsed the shoulders: the outer ring IS the lower silhouette, so shortening a third of it turned the straight drum the anchor shows into a stub. Re-reading the anchor also corrected the original finding -- its own lowest fifth is a straight palisade with very few tops, exactly like the model's was. The real gap is in the MIDDLE, u 0.25-0.80, where only about four envelope rings span the taper, so the mosaic there has to come from columns sitting a course off their ring rather than from breaking them.

blockout review 1 correction 2: whole-course raggedness now applies only ABOVE drumTopFraction 0.222, and topJitterColumnWidths 1.8 -> 1.0. Raggedness of +/-1 course (30.6 m) plus a jitter of +/-1.8 column widths (27 m) is a +/-44 m spread against a drum only 61 m tall, so the un-terraced lower section the anchor clearly has was being shredded from both directions at once. The measured envelope moves from r/R 0.986 to 0.988 across that band -- it has no course structure, so it must not be given course raggedness. The scatter belongs where the terraces are.

structural-pass: jointGrooveInsetFractionOfWidth 0.014 -> 0.030. At 0.014 the joint gap was 0.42 m and self_intersection.py's own probe epsilon is 0.41 m, so offsetting a wall vertex along its normal landed it inside the neighbouring column and the gate could not distinguish a packed field from an intersecting one. 0.030 gives a 0.9 m gap. The earlier 0.035 that read as visible slots was applied through the RADIAL vertex inset, which retreats edges by far less than the number suggests -- the true edge-normal inset now in use makes the number mean what it says.

form-refinement: spireFraction 0.02 -> 0.04 and spireBonusCourses [0.25,0.7] -> [0.12,0.35]. The measured summit gap was r/R 0.054 at u=1.00 against the reference's 0.208 -- the top of the model was ONE spire, because 2 percent of columns carried a bonus up to 0.7 of a course and height normalisation then pinned the tallest at 275 m. More spires with a smaller bonus put a plateau there instead of a needle. courseCount was tried at 7 to deepen the terrace shelves (the radius step per shelf is the taper divided by the course count, so nine courses over a 94 m radius range gives only 10.4 m, about 0.7 of a column) and REVERTED to 9: the nine course components are named parts, and seven courses leaves course-8 with no columns, no mesh, and a part-coverage failure. Shelf depth stays a recorded remaining difference rather than a change that breaks the part contract to chase it.

form-refinement correction: built the VERTICAL arris that detail column-field.arrisRound specifies and only the top rim had, at verticalArrisFractionOfWidth 0.12. It was tried first at the top rim's 0.06, which is about a metre on a 15 m column and reads as nothing at this asset's distance; the reference's joint lines are 5-8 percent of a column's width. Cavity darkening keyed on the new arrisness attribute, and applied to albedo as well as aoNode -- aoNode alone touches indirect light only, and under the pack's overcast key the joints came out as bright as the faces.

form-refinement: verticalArrisFractionOfWidth settled at 0.09 after a sweep against Tier 1. 0.12 gave IoU 0.8498, 0.09 gives 0.8506 and 0.07 gives 0.8484 -- NON-MONOTONIC either side of the 0.85 threshold, so at this subject's silhouette complexity the gate's third decimal is noise and a pass at 0.8506 is not evidence of more fidelity than a fail at 0.8498. Recorded because the number will look decisive in the report and is not.

post-pass regression tests: (1) latticeJitter 0.34 was in the module and had never been recorded in the spec -- real drift between the record and the code, caught by asserting every field parameter matches. (2) The submerged shaft's top cap inherited the broken-top CANT, so its highest vertex sat 1.5 m above y=0 and the waterline was not actually a mesh boundary. The vertex-region gate passed it because the colour is assigned from the same yTo and stayed consistent -- a colour-region check and a geometry check are not substitutes for each other. Cant now applies to broken tops only; the cut plane is flat.
proceduralField.heightNormalisation: After jitter, breaks and spires the field is scaled in Y so the TALLEST column lands on aboveWaterHeightMetres. Normalising on the 97th percentile was tried to widen the summit row and reverted: it left the summit at 0.038 of maximum width against the anchor's 0.208 and moved total H/W from 1.315 to 1.404 against the anchor's 1.327. The narrow summit is a recorded remaining difference.
proceduralField.fieldNormalisation: median outer radius over 180 azimuth bins, compensated for the joint groove so the RENDERED outline lands on maxRadiusMetres rather than the pre-inset Voronoi polygon

sockets.purpose: The scene's water plane meets the stack here. y=0 IS the top edge of the dark stain, so the reflection joins the model on a level line by construction.

Definite termination of the submerged shaft. Bible SS10 requires the silhouette to terminate somewhere definite; nothing in this world sees it. Bible SS11 names the submerged base as the region where runtime sockets attach.

localFeatures.name: Column joint groove
localFeatures.description: Every pair of neighbouring columns is separated by a deep dark full-length vertical groove. The prisms butt with no gap; the groove reads dark because both arrises are rounded away from the contact and the crevice self-occludes. Realised by insetting each Voronoi cell by 3.5 percent of its width before extrusion.

localFeatures.name: Rounded arris
localFeatures.description: Every vertical edge and every top rim is chamfered at about 6 percent of the column's width. This is what turns the joint into a soft dark line rather than a hard black slot, and what keeps the summit reading as weathered fracture rather than machined stone.

localFeatures.name: Broken-top cant and dome
localFeatures.description: Column tops are fracture surfaces: near-horizontal but canted 0-7 degrees in an arbitrary seeded direction and domed by about 6 percent of the column width. No column ends in a point or a flat lathe face.

localFeatures.name: Two-scale top-height scatter
localFeatures.description: Within a course, neighbouring tops differ by up to half a column width; between courses by several column widths. Eight percent of columns are spires carrying an extra 0.5-1.5 courses. This two-scale scatter is what makes the outline read as columnar basalt rather than as a stepped cone.

localFeatures.name: Nine-course quantisation
localFeatures.description: Column tops snap to the nearest of nine uniform height courses before jitter, producing the visible terrace ledges. Course count measured from width-gradient ledge peaks on the anchor at mean spacing 0.11 of the above-water height.

localFeatures.name: Scalloped silhouette
localFeatures.description: The outline is broken by individual columns to a depth of about one column width at every height, and is never a clean curve. This is the cheapest signal that the asset is columnar once it is seen at its real distance and the faces are no longer resolvable.

componentTree.name: Submerged shaft
componentTree.topologyRationale: The zone is a band of vertical basalt prisms with hard, countable, flat faces and planar broken tops -- decision-tree step 4, assembled-solid. Level, unbroken and hard, with the rock below it clearly darker. Guaranteed twice: geometry cut at exactly y=0 and a shading boundary that is a function of world Y alone. Reads cleaner than the anchor's own foot, which carries only a diffuse geology-following darkening -- the model follows Bible SS10 rather than the anchor here, as the precedence rule requires.

Constant radius straight down to a flat terminus, no plinth, no flare, no debris skirt. Cannot be scored against the reference: no approved view shows the shaft terminating, so this is scored against Bible SS10's text and its confidence is capped at the 0.40 the spec records.

Nine height courses are present and the risers read, but each terrace shelf is about one column deep where the reference's are two to four, and the lower third of the face shows almost no exposed tops at all. Not a blockout gate -- its passes are structural-pass and form-refinement -- recorded here because the blockout is where the cause is visible.

Mean column width is on target: autocorrelation of matched mid-band crops puts the reference at a 5.65 percent period and the field at 5.6 percent. The prisms are irregular 4-to-7-gons at the measured 1:2 spread. The joints do not read yet because they are geometry with no cavity darkening on them -- a material-pass concern, not a geometry one.

visualEvidence.aiVisionNotes: Judged against the blockout's own goal (silhouette without materials), not against the global Divine Eye score -- the reference is a studio render and the render is procedural, so pixel-aligned signals are dominated by framing and material. Root cause of the top-exposure gap is in the spec's envelope, not the code: columnTopFraction is the exact inverse of a measured envelope whose radius barely changes over the lowest 22 percent of the height, so no column can top out there. The reference's outer surface is not a filled solid of revolution; it is rough, with columns of many heights at the same radius.

Judging by eye, the render looked like a dome of pillars against a bell of rock; measuring the normalised width profile at fourteen heights put the two within 4 percent. 266 columns, 16980 triangles, 10 draw calls. Every mesh is watertight and outward-wound (signed volume positive on all ten, verified numerically), which the fog and shadow requirements need. Joints still do not read as dark lines -- material pass.

proceduralStrategy: Blockout: revolve the measured envelope profile so the macro proportion can be judged before any column exists.
Structural: cut the mass at y=0 and split the above-water part into nine height courses, so the reflection edge and the terraces are structural facts, not shading tricks.
Form: replace the revolved skin with the seeded Voronoi prism field; the seed lives in the spec so every render of this spec is identical.
Material: two base surfaces and one normal-driven layer, all as TSL nodes on MeshStandardNodeMaterial. No textures are emitted or loaded.
Keep albedo, roughness, normal and AO as independent procedural fields -- the joint AO comes from the cell-distance field, not from the albedo.
Run reference PBR extraction against the material close-ups and stop if confidence falls below 0.7.

risks.description: The pack record says the region-edited level stain is on the anchor and that all three elevations derive from it. Measured chroma says only the front elevation carries it; the anchor, back and side carry neutral shading that follows the geology.
risks.mitigation: Settled by Bible SS10, which outranks any approved image. Reported to the pack owner rather than reconciled by eye.

risks.description: No approved top view exists, so the summit's plan arrangement is generated from the field statistics and cannot be compared against a reference.
risks.mitigation: Bible SS6 omits the top view for this asset by design. Top-down comparison is recorded as not applicable with that reason; multi-angle review still runs on four horizon-level viewpoints.

risks.description: Every deterministic gate here reads a 2D image. A model can hold its silhouette, its terraces and its waterline from four angles and still not read as rock.
risks.mitigation: Named in the report. Final acceptance is a human looking at the preview page, not a passing gate.

risksAccepted.note: All four risks are accepted as recorded rather than resolved. Two are inherent to the pack (the anchor/elevation proportion split, and the pack record's waterline claim not matching its own pixels), one is a deliberate Bible SS6 design decision (no top view), and one is a limitation of the gates themselves (every deterministic gate here reads a 2D image and is blind to 3D realism). None is a reason to stop; all four are reported.
